venues.name: Apéro

credentials: Lewisham Awards 2025, Best Wine List & Best Chef
Cuisine Good Food Guide 2025, recognised

venues.name: Sky Tower
venues.note: Auckland's 328-metre spire and the tallest structure in the Southern Hemisphere, with three observation decks and glass floor panels that drop the eye straight to the street 186 metres below. On a clear day the view runs 80 kilometres over the Waitematā, the Hauraki Gulf islands and the ring of volcanic cones; take the family up at dusk for the city lighting up, then dine at the revolving Orbit 360 one floor down.
credentials: Tripadvisor Travellers' Choice, #1 Auckland attraction

venues.name: SkyWalk & SkyJump at the Sky Tower
venues.note: For the thrill-seeker in the family: a harnessed walk on a 1.2-metre ledge around the tower's rim at 192 metres with no handrails, or a wire-guided base-jump-style plunge at up to 85 km/h. Grandparents can watch in comfort from the observation deck while the teenagers step off the edge; both run on private timed slots.

venues.name: Auckland War Memorial Museum (Tāmaki Paenga Hira)
venues.note: A neoclassical temple crowning the Domain, holding the world's finest collection of Māori and Pacific treasures alongside a carved meeting house and a full-sized war canoe. Book the twice-daily Māori cultural performance of song, haka and story for a dignified, multi-generational introduction to the culture of the land, then take tea on the terrace over the harbour.

venues.name: Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki
venues.note: New Zealand's oldest and largest art institution, with a soaring kauri-canopy roof over 17,000 works spanning European masters, contemporary New Zealand painting and a moving room of Māori ancestral portraits by Goldie and Lindauer. Entry to the permanent collection is free and it sits at the edge of Albert Park, an easy, cultured hour for any age.
credentials: World Building of the Year 2013 (World Architecture Festival)

venues.name: Viaduct Harbour
venues.note: The former America's Cup basin, now a ring of superyachts, waterside restaurants and champagne bars where Auckland comes to be seen. It is the natural place to base an evening on the water and the departure point for private charters and the America's Cup sailing yachts.

venues.name: Wynyard Quarter & Silo Park
venues.note: A reclaimed industrial waterfront turned promenade of playgrounds, seafood restaurants and the landmark red Silo Park, with summer outdoor cinema and night markets among the old cement silos. A relaxed, stroller-friendly stretch to walk off dinner as the harbour lights come on.

venues.name: America's Cup Sailing on the Waitematā
venues.note: Take the helm or simply recline on the rail of a genuine former America's Cup grand-prix racing yacht as it heels across the harbour past the Harbour Bridge and skyline. No experience needed and the whole family can crew or watch; private full-boat charters make it a discreet, unforgettable two hours on the City of Sails.

venues.name: Auckland Harbour Bridge Climb
venues.note: A guided harnessed walk up the arch of the 1959 road bridge to the summit at 65 metres, with the Waitematā, the yachts and Rangitoto laid out beneath you. There is also a bungy off a purpose-built pod for the daring; the climb itself is a gentle, steady ascent suitable for confident older children and grandparents alike.

venues.name: Mission Bay & Tamaki Drive
venues.note: Auckland's most beloved seaside promenade, a golden crescent of beach with an Art Deco fountain, gelato and waterfront cafés looking straight across to Rangitoto. Drive or cycle the full sweep of Tamaki Drive past the yacht basins for the classic City of Sails afternoon; easy and safe for all ages.

venues.name: Bastion Point & the Michael Joseph Savage Memorial
venues.note: A clifftop of consecrated ground above Tamaki Drive, its Art Deco obelisk and formal gardens giving a sweeping panorama over the harbour to Rangitoto. It is also one of the most significant sites in modern Māori history, scene of the 506-day 1977–78 land occupation; a quiet, contemplative stop with a story worth a guide.

venues.name: Maungawhau / Mount Eden
venues.note: Auckland's highest volcanic cone at 196 metres, with a perfect grassy crater at the top and a full 360-degree sweep of the isthmus and both harbours. Walking to the summit is protected as an ancestral maunga, but the reward is the definitive view of the volcanic city; keep to the paths as the crater is sacred.

venues.name: Maungakiekie / One Tree Hill & Cornwall Park
venues.note: A 182-metre cone crowned by an obelisk and ringed by the largest pre-European earthwork fortifications on earth, set in the gifted parkland of Cornwall Park with grazing sheep and centenarian oaks. A gentle drive or walk to the summit and a picnic under the trees make an idyllic, unhurried family morning.

venues.name: Auckland Domain & the Wintergardens
venues.note: The city's oldest park, spread over an ancient volcano, with the Wintergardens' twin Edwardian glasshouses of tropical and cool-climate blooms and a fern-filled sunken quarry. A serene, shaded stroll that pairs naturally with the Museum on the same hill.

venues.name: Karangahape Road (K' Road)
venues.note: Auckland's most characterful strip, a mile of vintage stores, galleries, tiny wine bars and cuisines from Malaysian to modern Brazilian, named among the world's coolest streets by Time Out. Go for the atmosphere and the food rather than luxury shopping; it is bohemian, alive and refreshingly unpolished.
credentials: Time Out, World's Coolest Streets 2022

venues.name: Ponsonby Road
venues.note: Nicknamed 'the dining room of Auckland', a village high street of Victorian villas turned into the city's densest run of good restaurants, cafés and design boutiques, anchored by the food-hall energy of Ponsonby Central. The place to spend a leisurely lunch and afternoon; several kitchens handle vegetarian and Indian palates well.

venues.name: Britomart Precinct
venues.note: The sleekest quarter of the central city, a cluster of restored heritage warehouses now holding New Zealand designer boutiques, top restaurants and the design-led Hotel Britomart, steps from the ferry terminal. The natural base for a stylish, walkable stay and a Saturday morning market.

venues.name: SEA LIFE Kelly Tarlton's Aquarium
venues.note: Built into old harbourside sewage tanks by a New Zealand diving pioneer, with curved underwater tunnels of sharks and stingrays and an Antarctic ice enclosure of penguins. A reliable, weather-proof couple of hours that delights younger children on Tamaki Drive.

venues.name: New Zealand Maritime Museum (Hui Te Ananui a Tangaroa)
venues.note: On Hobson Wharf beside the Viaduct, tracing the ocean story from the first Polynesian voyagers to America's Cup glory, with heritage vessels moored outside that still sail the harbour. A short guided sail on a classic scow or steamer is the highlight for a maritime-minded family.

venues.name: Waiheke Island, vineyards, beaches & Oneroa
venues.note: A 40-minute ferry to a warmer, sunnier island of forty white-sand beaches and world-class vineyards, where cellar doors like Mudbrick, Cable Bay and Stonyridge serve Bordeaux-style reds over Hauraki Gulf views back to the skyline. The essential Auckland day trip; a private driver-guide or helicopter transfer lets multi-generational groups linger over long lunches without watching the clock.

venues.name: Mudbrick Vineyard
venues.note: On Waiheke's northern tip, a rose-garden estate with sweeping Hauraki Gulf views to the Auckland skyline, a celebrated restaurant and cottages for those who want to stay the night. The most photographed cellar door on the island and a favourite for a special-occasion lunch.

venues.name: Man O' War Vineyards
venues.note: At the wild eastern end of Waiheke, a beachfront tasting room reached by a scenic drive through the island's largest private estate, pouring single-vineyard wines feet from the sand. Remote and unhurried; charter a boat or helicopter in for the most discreet arrival.

venues.name: Rangitoto Island Summit Track
venues.note: The perfect volcanic cone that frames every Auckland postcard, a 600-year-old island reached by a 25-minute ferry, climbed in about an hour through the world's largest pōhutukawa forest and black lava fields to a 259-metre crater rim. The summit view over the gulf and city is superb; bring a torch for the lava caves and sun protection for the exposed scoria.

venues.name: Tiritiri Matangi Island Open Sanctuary
venues.note: One of the world's great conservation successes, a predator-free island where you walk among some of New Zealand's rarest birds in the wild, takahē, kōkako, saddleback and stitchbird, that exist almost nowhere else so freely. A guided day with an island volunteer is a quiet privilege for nature-lovers; the ferry runs only Wednesday to Sunday, so book ahead.

venues.name: Devonport & Mount Victoria
venues.note: A 12-minute ferry to a genteel Victorian seaside village of bookshops, cafés and colonial villas, with the little cone of Mount Victoria offering a postcard view straight back to the city skyline. An effortless, charming half-day that even the least mobile of the party can enjoy from the waterfront.

venues.name: North Head (Maungauika)
venues.note: A headland cone above Devonport honeycombed with Victorian coastal-defence tunnels and gun emplacements, guarding the harbour entrance with commanding views over the gulf. A gentle walk-up with just enough history and dark passages to intrigue children.

venues.name: Waitākere Ranges Regional Park
venues.note: Sixteen thousand hectares of native rainforest, kauri stands and waterfalls dropping to the wild west coast, half an hour from the city. Note that a kauri-dieback protection programme has closed many forest tracks, go with a guide who knows what is open, and always use the boot-cleaning stations to protect the ancient trees.

venues.name: Piha Beach
venues.note: The most famous of Auckland's black-sand surf beaches, a dramatic ironsand crescent guarded by the great hulk of Lion Rock and pounded by Tasman swell. Wild, cinematic and beautiful, but the rips are serious, so swim only between the summer patrol flags and consider it a place to watch the surf rather than brave it.

venues.name: Karekare Beach
venues.note: The most secluded of the west-coast beaches, reached through rainforest and a stream crossing, its vast empty ironsand made famous as the setting of the Oscar-winning film The Piano. Utterly atmospheric and almost always deserted; there are no facilities, so come prepared.

venues.name: Muriwai Beach & the Gannet Colony
venues.note: A rugged black-sand coast where, from August to March, some 1,200 Australasian gannets nest on the clifftop at Ōtakamiro Point within metres of easy viewing platforms, an extraordinary wildlife spectacle with no effort required. Pair it with lunch at the nearby winery for a full west-coast morning.

venues.name: Hunua Falls
venues.note: A 30-metre waterfall spilling into a bush-fringed pool in the Hūnua Ranges, under an hour southeast of the city and far quieter than the western beaches. A short, easy path and a picnic make it a gentle escape into native forest; check current track status before you go.

venues.name: Matakana Village & Wine Country
venues.note: An hour north, a village of boutique galleries, a beloved Saturday farmers' market and a cluster of small wineries such as Brick Bay, whose sculpture trail winds through native bush and ponds. A civilised, low-key alternative to Waiheke for a day among vines, art and artisan food.

venues.name: Tāwharanui Regional Park
venues.note: An open sanctuary on a peninsula north of the city, ringing white-sand Anchor Bay with predator-proof fencing so that takahē roam the grassland and kiwi call at night. Among the finest beaches in the Auckland region and blissfully uncrowded on a weekday.

venues.name: Goat Island Marine Reserve
venues.note: New Zealand's first no-take marine reserve, established in 1975 near Leigh, where snapper, crayfish and rays crowd the shallows for snorkellers and a glass-bottomed boat. A rewarding half-day for families who want to see the sea life without diving; go on a calm, offshore-wind day for clear water.
credentials: New Zealand's first marine reserve (est. 1975)

venues.name: Te Hana Te Ao Marama Cultural Centre
venues.note: An hour north, Auckland's leading Māori cultural centre, where a traditional welcome, a guided walk through a replica fortified pā, a kapa haka performance and a hāngī earth-oven feast give a genuine, unhurried immersion. Arranged as a private group visit it is a dignified highlight for multi-generational travellers.

venues.name: Waka Voyaging Experience
venues.note: Paddle a waka hourua, a Māori ocean-going canoe, on the Waitematā with the Te Toki Voyaging Trust, learning traditional star-and-swell navigation from the descendants of the Pacific's greatest wayfinders. A rare, hands-on cultural encounter on the water rather than a staged show.

venues.name: Waitomo Glowworm Caves (day trip)
venues.note: About 2.5 hours south, a limestone cavern where you glide by boat beneath a ceiling of thousands of glowworms glimmering like a private galaxy, one of New Zealand's singular natural wonders. Best done as a private full-day drive, often combined with Hobbiton; the black-water rafting option is for the adventurous.

venues.name: Hobbiton Movie Set, Matamata (day trip)
venues.note: Two hours south, the immaculately kept Shire from the Lord of the Rings and Hobbit films, forty-four hobbit holes set in green Waikato farmland, ending with a drink at the Green Dragon Inn. A joyful, easy day for film-lovers and children; a private car and guide beats the coach tours for pace.

venues.name: Coromandel Peninsula & Cathedral Cove (day trip)
venues.note: About two hours east, a coast of pōhutukawa-fringed coves crowned by the great natural rock arch of Cathedral Cove and the geothermal quirk of Hot Water Beach, where you dig your own warm spa in the sand. A long but rewarding day; helicopter transfer turns it into an effortless outing and avoids the winding roads.

venues.name: Rotorua Geothermal & Māori Culture (long day trip)
venues.note: Around three hours south, the heart of Māori tourism and geothermal drama, bubbling mud, geysers, thermal spas and the living village of Whakarewarewa. It is a stretch as a single day, so most travellers stay a night; a helicopter or charter flight makes a day visit civilised.

venues.name: Bay of Islands (overnight-worthy trip)
venues.note: Roughly three hours north, a sub-tropical seascape of 144 islands, dolphin cruises, big-game fishing and the founding site of the nation at Waitangi. Truly it deserves an overnight, but a scenic flight or helicopter from Auckland can deliver a memorable single day of sailing and history.

venues.name: Scenic Helicopter Flight over the Hauraki Gulf
venues.note: Lift off from the waterfront or Ardmore for a private flight over the skyline, Rangitoto's crater and the vineyards of Waiheke, landing for a cellar-door lunch or a remote beach. The most discreet and time-efficient way for a family to see the City of Sails and reach the gulf islands in style.

venues.name: Auckland Fish Market & Wynyard dining
venues.note: A working fish market turned food destination on the waterfront, with oyster bars, a sushi counter and cooking classes celebrating the day's catch from the Hauraki Gulf. A lively, casual counterpoint to the fine-dining rooms and a good place to understand New Zealand seafood.

venues.name: Paris Butter
venues.note: One of Auckland's most refined tables, French technique applied to the best New Zealand produce across an ever-changing tasting menu in an elegant Herne Bay villa. The kind of hushed, special-occasion dinner discerning travellers seek; advise the kitchen of any vegetarian or Jain needs when booking.
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Three Hats

venues.name: Sidart
venues.note: Chef Sid Sahrawat's flagship degustation room above Ponsonby, a long-running standard-bearer for creative fine dining in the city with polished wine pairings and warm service. Sahrawat's Indian heritage runs through his kitchens, so it is a considered choice for Indian palates seeking a tasting-menu evening.
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards, Three Hats (long-standing)

venues.name: Cassia
venues.note: Sid Sahrawat's celebrated modern Indian restaurant, refined, contemporary cooking rooted in the subcontinent that has long topped Auckland's lists, a rare fine-dining Indian table of genuine ambition. Confirm the current location when booking, as the restaurant has relocated from its long-time SkyCity home.

venues.name: Auckland Zoo
venues.note: A well-regarded conservation zoo beside Western Springs park, with a night-time kiwi house where families can finally see New Zealand's shy national bird, plus native tuatara and a strong Australasian collection. An easy, shaded day for younger children.

venues.name: Albert Park & the University Quarter
venues.note: A formal Victorian park of fountains, statues and flowerbeds set between the Art Gallery and the university, a green pause in the heart of the city. A pretty, unhurried stroll to link a museum morning with lunch on High Street.

venues.name: Motuihe & Motutapu Islands
venues.note: Quieter neighbours to Rangitoto and Waiheke, predator-free islands of white-sand bays and gentle walking tracks that see a fraction of the crowds. Ideal for a private boat picnic day when you want the gulf to yourselves.

venues.name: Caretaker
venues.note: A New York-inspired basement speakeasy beneath Britomart, no menu, just a host who reads you and pours the perfect drink, with live jazz early in the week.
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery listed
A landmark Auckland cocktail bar (est. 2015)

venues.name: Deadshot
venues.note: Caretaker's cooler, moodier sibling, effortlessly stylish, seated-only and welcoming, where you are led in once a table is free.
credentials: From the Caretaker stable, a benchmark Auckland cocktail lineage
A landmark Britomart cocktail bar

venues.name: Panacea
venues.note: An inner-city cocktail kitchen and whisky bar with a sustainability ethos, inventive drinks and a serious spirits collection.
credentials: Lewisham Awards 2025, Best Cocktail Experience
Lewisham Awards 2025, Best Sustainability

venues.name: Annabel's
venues.note: A relaxed, characterful Ponsonby bar with a chilled vibe, live music, wine launches and guest-chef pop-ups in a much-loved neighbourhood room.
credentials: A landmark Ponsonby Road bar
Editorially recognised, Urban List / Denizen Auckland

venues.name: The Rooftop at QT
venues.note: A glamorous rooftop terrace over the Viaduct marina, cocktails, colour and one of the best harbour views in the city.
credentials: Atop QT Auckland, a landmark Viaduct rooftop bar
